newsitem.title: UK: Russian ratings bode well for debut Eurobond.
newsitem.headline: Russian ratings bode well for debut Eurobond.

text.p: Russia's long-awaited return to international capital markets was given a fillip on Monday by a batch of better-than-expected credit ratings.
"They (ratings) augur well for the expected Eurobond," a syndicate manager close to the deal said.
"It is clearly very positive. A few months ago there was talk about single B, but clearly we're quite a way from that."
Moody's Investors Service set a Ba2 ceiling for long-term foreign-currency bonds issued by Russian borrowers.
Standard & Poor's Corp gave Russia a BB- long-term sovereign rating, while European credit rating agency IBCA gave it a BB+ long-term foreign currency rating.
All three ratings are non-investment grade.
"Moody's rating is the same as Mexico's, S&P's is the same as Argentina and the IBCA rating is extremely strong," said the syndicate source close to the issue.
J.P. Morgan and SBC Warburg have long held the mandate for Russia's debut Eurobond. An initial tranche of up to $500 million with a three- to five-year maturity was expected.

Another syndicate manager close to the bond said: "We're delighted with the ratings...they're fantastic. This will help the Russians in their efforts to access the capital markets at a cost-effective rate."
"It is certainly what the country deserves, although it is better than the market expected," he added.
IBCA managing director Christopher Huhne told Reuters Financial Television its BB+ rating was the highest level of speculative-grade ratings.
"It compares to Uruguay, it is just below Hungary, Tunisia, Slovakia and just above Romania, South Africa, Turkey and Brazil."
Huhne said Russia was an unusually difficult credit to rate given the considerable political risks.

"If President Boris Yeltsin dies or is incapacitated and there is an early election within the next year, then it is possible that there would be a populist or a communist-supported candidate who might win," he added.
Huhne said this could mean two- or three-years of lost progress, slow growth and macroeconomic instability.
Last week, Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin said the country would launch its inaugural Eurobond after receiving a credit rating.
"We would like to issue the first tranche with a rating," Potanin said.

Moscow has also announced plans for its debut international bond -- expected to be around $300 million -- which was expected to follow the launch of Russia's bond. C.S. First Boston and Nomura have been mandated to lead manage the transaction.
